L20@P0: A binary tensor consists of 2n entries arranged into hypercube
L21@P0: format 2 × 2 ×··· × 2. There are n ways to flatten such a
L22@P0: tensor into a matrix of size 2 × 2n−1. For each flattening, M,
L23@P0: we take the determinant of its Gram matrix, det(MMT ). We
L24@P0: consider the map that sends a tensor to its n-tuple of Gram
L25@P0: determinants. We propose a semi-algebraic characterization
L26@P0: of the image of this map. This offers an answer to a question
L27@P0: raised by Hackbusch and Uschmajew concerning the higherorder singular values of tensors.

L29@P0: 1. Introduction
L30@P0: The Gram determinants of a real binary tensor of format 2 × 2 ×···× 2(n times)
L31@P0: are an n-tuple of quadratic invariants of the tensor. We introduce the Gram locus, the
L32@P0: locus of tuples that arise as the Gram determinants of a real binary tensor. Here, the
L33@P0: Gram locus is equal to the “set of feasible higher-order singular values”, from [8], under
L34@P0: change of coordinates. The Gram determinants offer a convenient set of coordinates for
L35@P0: studying the higher order singular values of a tensor.

L39@P1: In Theorem 1.3 we find the convex hull of the Gram locus for real binary tensors. It
L40@P1: is a convex polytope that we describe explicitly. Its facet defining inequalities are that
L41@P1: each Gram determinant is bounded by the sum of the others. We give a sum-of-squares
L42@P1: proof. In Theorem 1.4, we express the Gram locus as a semi-algebraic set for the case of
L43@P1: 2 × 2 × 2 tensors. The semi-algebraic description determines whether a tuple lies in the
L44@P1: Gram locus or its complement, and characterizes tuples on the boundary. The non-linear
L45@P1: part of the boundary of the Gram locus is Fig. 4, and it is depicted in the highest higher
L46@P1: order singular value coordinates in Fig. 6.
L47@P1: In Section 1 of [8] it is conjectured that tensors with strictly decreasing and positive
L48@P1: singular values in each flattening lie in the interior of the feasible set. Example 3.1 is
L49@P1: a counter-example to this conjecture. It is a tensor on the boundary of the feasible set
L50@P1: whose higher order singular values in each flattening are distinct and positive. Its singular
L51@P1: values are located at the black dot in Fig. 6.
L52@P1: Conjecture 1.5 proposes the general form for the Gram locus. It has a concise expression as the non-negativity of a single polynomial in the Gram determinants.
L53@P1: Finally, Section 4 gives a partial answer to [8, Problem 1.6], characterizing the tensors
L54@P1: whose higher order singular values coincide. In the case of matrices agreement of singular
L55@P1: values implies orthogonal equivalence, but this is not true for tensors. Theorem 4.1 shows
L56@P1: that the hyperdeterminant bridges the gap between orthogonal equivalence of tensors and
L57@P1: agreement of the higher order singular value decomposition in the 2 × 2 × 2 case. Our
L58@P1: set-up for the 2 × 2 × 2 tensor format is described in the following example.

L125@P2: The Gram determinant map G gives the higher order singular values of a binary tensor,
L126@P2: as follows. The higher order singular values of a tensor, introduced in [5], are the singular
L127@P2: values of its n principal flattenings, the non-negative square roots of the eigenvalues of
L128@P2: the n Gram matrices. Just as the singular values of a matrix describe it up to orthogonal
L129@P2: change of basis, via the singular value decomposition (SVD), the higher order singular
L130@P2: values give the corresponding multilinear structure of a tensor, via the higher order
L131@P2: singular value decomposition (HOSVD). The trace of any Gram matrix, t, is the sum
L132@P2: of the squares of the entries of the original tensor, its squared Frobenius norm, hence is
L133@P2: unchanged by the choice of flattening. Thus the higher order singular values from the
L134@P2: ith flattening are the non-negative solutions to the univariate polynomial in x:
L135@P2: x4 − tx2 + di.

L151@P3: Characterizing feasible combinations of higher order singular values is an open problem [8, Problem 1.4]. In this paper we use the Gram locus to make progress towards its
L152@P3: solution.
L153@P3: For any combination of Gram determinants, a dimension count shows there generically
L154@P3: exists a (2n − n)-dimensional family of complex tensors whose image under G is those
L155@P3: determinants. We seek a real tensor in the pre-image. The parts of the image of G
L156@P3: where some di almost vanishes are of particular interest: these are tensors which can be
L157@P3: approximated to good accuracy by a tensor of smaller flattening rank than its dimension,
L158@P3: as in [6].
L159@P3: We note that the analogue of the Gram determinants can also be studied in the case
L160@P3: of hierarchical tensor representations, including the Tensor Train (TT)/Matrix Product
L161@P3: State representation [7, Chapter 12]. The size of the TT format required to represent a
L162@P3: tensor is given by the ranks of the flattenings obtained by grouping the first j indices for
L163@P3: the rows, with the remaining indices forming the columns, for 1 ≤ j ≤ d − 1. A tensor
L164@P3: being representable by a TT format with deficient jth bond dimension is equivalent to
L165@P3: the determinant at that flattening vanishing.
